label: Blue Note
rationale: A hallmark Dexter Gordon Blue Note date from his peak 1960s period — recorded in 1965 between Go (1962) and Gettin' Around (1965), though not released until 1979 as part of Blue Note's LT Series. The session teams Gordon with Freddie Hubbard, Barry Harris, Bob Cranshaw, and Billy Higgins — a frontline of proven chemistry (Hubbard and Gordon had just recorded One Flight Up). The Penguin Guide gives it 2.5 stars (its 'good' threshold), DownBeat 4 stars, Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 4 stars, and Robert Christgau called it 'superb mature late bebop'. As one of Dexter Gordon's essential Blue Note sessions from his mid-60s prime — a period already represented in the canon by Go! and Our Man in Paris — Clubhouse fills a gap in Gordon's studio arc. AllMusic calls it Hard Bop.

personnel_record.notes: Single session on May 27, 1965 at Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs. Not released until 1979 on Blue Note LT-989. Engineer Rudy Van Gelder inferred (inf) — all Blue Note sessions at Van Gelder Studio in this era were engineered by Rudy Van Gelder. Freddie Hubbard absent from 'Jodi' (track 6). Ben Tucker substitutes for Bob Cranshaw on bass on 'Devilette' (track 3), which Tucker also composed. Recorded the day before the Gettin' Around session (May 28-29). AllMusic lists Rudy Van Gelder under 'Remastering' for the RVG CD edition, confirming his association with the session.

ballot.case_for: This is an exceptionally strong 1965 Blue Note session: Dexter Gordon and Freddie Hubbard are supported by Barry Harris, Bob Cranshaw or Ben Tucker, and Billy Higgins, with the dossier documenting the track-level personnel from S1 and S3. The Gordon-Hubbard frontline has established chemistry from One Flight Up, while the music offers immediate discovery value through Gordon's mature tenor, a ballad, blues, and swinging hard-bop originals. It also fills a genuine mid-1960s gap between Gordon's already canonical Our Man in Paris and Go! and the next-day Gettin' Around session, even if the same-artist recurrence is not itself a negative under the rubric.
ballot.case_against: Clubhouse was shelved until 1979, so it had no influence on the crucial 1960s hard-bop lineage and functions primarily as an archival supplement to Gordon's better-known statements. It is a conventional blowing date rather than a defining Gordon album, and the dossier's strongest reception claims—DownBeat and Rolling Stone four-star ratings and Christgau's praise—are not actually supported by the six listed source tokens; the only stated Penguin rating is 2.5 stars, suggesting a good but nonessential record. Its personnel and playing are excellent, but the album adds little to the post-bebop story that Go!, Our Man in Paris, or Gettin' Around do not represent more decisively.
ballot.disagreement: The references agree that the session is in scope and musically strong, but they split on the final tier: Reference 1 judged it contested and worth considering, emphasizing session gravity and discovery value, while Reference 2 recommended exclude_suggested because the delayed archival release, weak consensus, and lack of defining or historical impact outweigh the performance quality.
ballot.recommendation: Keep Clubhouse as a consider-level borderline candidate for John's listening queue, but do not treat it as a canon priority unless its reception evidence or distinctive musical value proves stronger than the dossier currently shows.
